segments.text: Health psychology studies how behaviour, beliefs, emotions and social conditions relate to health, illness and healthcare. It does not replace medicine; it adds psychological and behavioural understanding to health-related questions.
The central idea is the biopsychosocial view: health outcomes can reflect interactions among biological, psychological and social factors.

items.text: Health beliefs and behaviour
: People’s beliefs about risk, seriousness, benefits, barriers and their own ability to act can influence behaviours such as seeking care, exercising or following treatment.
Models of health psychology

: The biopsychosocial model integrates biological, psychological and social influences. Health-behaviour models such as the Health Belief Model or planned-behaviour approaches help explain why knowledge alone does not always change behaviour.
Assessment and intervention

: Assessment may examine stress, coping, health beliefs, adherence, behaviour and social support. Interventions may include education, behaviour change, coping skills, motivational approaches and support for treatment adherence.
Models of stress

: Stress can be viewed as a response, a demanding event, or a transaction between demands and a person’s appraisal/resources. The transactional approach emphasizes how the same event may be experienced differently by different people.
Chronic and terminal illness

: Long-term or terminal illness can affect identity, mood, family roles, work, adherence and quality of life. Psychological care may support coping, communication and adjustment alongside medical care.
Social support
: Emotional, informational and practical support can help people cope with illness and stress. The quality and appropriateness of support matter, not merely the number of contacts.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

Health psychology studies how biological processes interact with behaviour, cognition, emotion and social conditions. The biopsychosocial model is not a claim that every disease has a psychological cause. It is a framework for asking how multiple levels influence risk, prevention, treatment adherence, coping and quality of life.

items.text: Biological level
: Disease processes, genetics, immune function and physical condition directly matter.
Psychological level
: Beliefs, habits, stress appraisal, coping and emotion can influence behaviour and physiological regulation.
Social level
: Income, work, family support, culture, healthcare access and social inequality affect exposure to risks and capacity to respond.

blocks.text: Why knowledge does not automatically change behaviour

items.text: Health Belief Model

: Behaviour is influenced by perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, expected benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action and self-efficacy. Someone may understand a risk yet still not act if barriers appear greater than benefits.
Theory of planned behaviour
: Intentions are shaped by attitudes, perceived social norms and perceived behavioural control. Intentions predict behaviour imperfectly because opportunities and habits also matter.
Self-efficacy
: Belief in one's capability to perform a health behaviour influences initiation and persistence. Effective interventions build manageable mastery experiences rather than relying only on warnings.
Habit and environment
: Repeated behaviour becomes easier when cues and environments support it. Structural interventions such as making healthy options accessible can complement education.
Stress as stimulus
: Some approaches classify external demands or life events as stressors. The limitation is that the same event can be experienced differently by different people.
Stress as response
: Physiological and emotional reactions can be studied directly. This captures bodily consequences but may ignore meaning and context.
Transactional model

: Lazarus and Folkman emphasized appraisal: people evaluate whether an event threatens important goals and whether coping resources are sufficient. Stress therefore emerges from a person-environment transaction.
Problem-focused coping
: Attempts to change the stressor or one's practical relationship to it, for example planning or seeking information.
Emotion-focused coping
: Attempts to regulate emotional distress when the situation cannot immediately be changed. Neither category is always superior; effectiveness depends on controllability and context.

blocks.text: Chronic illness, adherence and social support

items.text: Adherence
: Following a treatment plan depends on understanding, side effects, cost, routines, beliefs, communication and access. Labelling non-adherence as simple irresponsibility overlooks these barriers.
Chronic illness
: Long-term illness can affect identity, work, family roles and mood. Psychological support can improve coping and self-management without replacing medical treatment.
Terminal illness
: Care may focus on communication, symptom coping, family support, meaning and quality of life. Psychological work should respect patient preferences and the realities of medical prognosis.
Social support
: Emotional, informational and practical support can buffer stress and improve coping, but unwanted or controlling support may be ineffective. Quality and fit matter more than the number of contacts.

rows: Avoid this error Do not imply that illness is caused by a person’s attitude alone. Biological disease processes are real; psychology examines behavioural and psychosocial influences alongside them.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define health psychology, introduce the biopsychosocial model, explain beliefs/behaviour, stress models, assessment/intervention, chronic illness and social support.
• Lazarus & Folkman, Stress, Appraisal, and Coping (1984).
• Health behaviour is shaped by more than knowledge.
• Stress depends partly on appraisal and coping resources.
• Psychological intervention can complement medical treatment.
• Social support can affect coping and treatment behaviour.
